paragraphs.heading: How much life the sea holds
paragraphs.text: As of 2023, more than 242,000 species living in the sea had been documented. Perhaps two million more have yet to be documented. Researchers describe about 2,300 new marine species in an average year. Today's marine species run from microscopic phytoplankton to huge cetaceans such as the blue whale, which can reach 33 m in length.

paragraphs.heading: The biggest living space on Earth
paragraphs.text: The ocean covers 71 percent of the world's surface and averages nearly 3.7 kilometres deep. Measured by volume, it supplies about 90 percent of the planet's living space. By convention the planet is split into five separate oceans, but they all join into a single world ocean. The deepest underwater spot is Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench in the Pacific Ocean, at a depth of 10,900 metres.

paragraphs.heading: What sea water is like
paragraphs.text: About 97.5% of Earth's water is saline, and the other 2.5% is fresh water. On average, a kilogram of seawater in Earth's oceans holds about 35 grams of salt, or 3.5% salt. Most of that salt comes from rocks on land as they weather and erode. Some salts are released by volcanic activity or extracted from cool igneous rocks. The oceans also hold dissolved gases from the atmosphere, which many aquatic life forms need to survive.

paragraphs.heading: Where life started
paragraphs.text: The earliest known life forms were archaea and bacteria. They evolved in the Archean oceans around deep sea hydrothermal vents. In the early Proterozoic, an episode called the Great Oxygenation Event significantly changed the chemistry of the sea. Complex life eventually arose in the sea during the Neoproterozoic. The early Phanerozoic then brought a prominent burst of evolution known as the Cambrian Explosion, when actively moving creatures called eumetazoans became prevalent.

paragraphs.heading: What marine life does for the planet
paragraphs.text: Microorganisms make up most of the living matter in the sea: estimates put them at about 70% or about 90% of total marine biomass. Marine primary producers, mainly cyanobacteria and algae with chloroplasts, make oxygen and lock away carbon through photosynthesis. This generates enormous biomass and significantly influences the chemistry of the atmosphere. Marine life also in part shapes and protects shorelines. Some organisms, such as corals, even help make new land through accumulated reef-building.

paragraphs.heading: The ocean and the weather
paragraphs.text: Sea water strongly influences the climate of the world, with the oceans acting as a large store of heat. Shifts in how temperature is spread through the ocean can cause significant shifts in weather. The El Niño-Southern Oscillation is one such shift.

paragraphs.heading: An ocean on another world
paragraphs.text: Water is found elsewhere in the Solar System too. Europa, a moon of Jupiter slightly smaller than Earth's Moon, has a strong possibility of a large saltwater ocean beneath its ice surface. Estimates put the outer crust of solid ice at about 10–30 km thick and the liquid ocean below it at about 100 km deep. That would give Europa's ocean over twice the volume of Earth's ocean. There has been speculation that it could support life.
